notes.meaning: Bezalel, Oholiab, and every skilled craftsman were called to build the tabernacle. God had given them the skill, understanding, and wisdom to carry out all the holy work. They went straight to work with joy, eager to obey everything the Lord had ordered.

Moses formally gathered Bezalel, Oholiab, and the skilled workers whose hearts were moved to take part. Natural skill was not enough on its own; God gave them special ability and a willing spirit to serve. In the same way, God calls people whose hearts are ready to do his work.

The craftsmen received from Moses all the supplies the Israelites had donated for the sanctuary. Even while the work was moving forward, the people kept bringing freewill offerings morning after morning. Moses handed over every gift honestly, keeping nothing back for himself.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The people's eager morning giving was seen partly as a sign of true repentance, making amends for how freely they had once handed over gold to make the golden calf.

notes.meaning: The builders stopped what they were doing and came together to speak to Moses. They explained that the people were bringing far more supplies than the project needed. The craftsmen showed great honesty and integrity by refusing to stockpile or keep extra materials for themselves.

Moses sent a public announcement throughout the camp telling everyone to stop making or bringing more gifts. The people obeyed and stopped giving because there was already more than enough on hand. God's people gave so cheerfully and abundantly that leadership had to tell them to stop.

The craftsmen began constructing the tabernacle by making ten inner curtains out of fine linen and colorful blue, purple, and scarlet yarn. Skillful weavers embroidered figures of cherubim, which are winged heavenly beings, into the fabric. Each curtain was the exact same size, and the workers stitched them into two wide sets of five.

The workers made fifty loops of blue cord along the edge of each five-curtain set. They lined up the loops on each side and fastened them together with fifty gold clasps. This linked the pieces so perfectly that the tabernacle roof formed a single, unified canopy.

Next, the workers wove eleven curtains of goat hair to create a tent covering over the fine linen tabernacle. These goat-hair curtains were thirty cubits long and four cubits wide, making them slightly larger to protect the inner layer. Five curtains were joined into one set and the other six into another.

The craftsmen added fifty loops along the edge of each set of goat-hair curtains. They made fifty bronze clasps to snap the loops together into one large sheet. Bronze was used here instead of gold because this covering was further away from the holy inner room.

The builders made two additional protective roof coverings to place over the goat hair. The lower layer was made of tough ram skins dyed red, and the outermost layer was made of durable leather skins. These tough layers shielded the sacred dwelling from harsh desert weather.

The workers shaped standing frames out of strong acacia wood to form the walls of the tabernacle. Each frame was ten cubits high and one and a half cubits wide, with two wooden pegs at the bottom. Every single board was carved in the exact same pattern so the walls would stand straight and even.

The craftsmen set up twenty wooden frames along the south side of the tabernacle. Underneath the frames, they poured forty heavy silver bases, with two bases anchoring the two pegs of each wooden frame. These solid silver footings kept the wood off the desert ground and held the structure firm.

The builders made twenty matching wooden frames for the north side of the tabernacle. Just like the south side, this wall rested on forty silver bases, with two bases supporting each upright frame. This gave both long sides of the building identical strength and beauty.

For the back wall of the tabernacle facing west, the builders made six frames, plus two special corner frames. These corner frames were locked together from bottom to top and held tight by a single ring. In all, the rear wall had eight frames standing in sixteen heavy silver bases.

The workers cut wooden crossbars of acacia to slide through gold rings on the frames and tie the walls together. Five bars ran along the south wall, five along the north wall, and five across the western rear wall. The center bar ran straight through the middle of the frames from end to end, and all the frames and bars were overlaid with pure gold.

The craftsmen wove the inner veil out of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and fine linen, embroidering it with winged cherubim. This heavy curtain hung from gold hooks on four gold-covered acacia posts set in silver bases. It served as a sacred divider between the Holy Place and the Most Holy Place, reminding worshippers of the holiness of God's presence.

For the front entrance of the tent, the workers embroidered a colorful curtain of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and fine linen. This entrance screen hung on five acacia posts whose tops and bands were overlaid with gold. Unlike the inner veil that stood in silver, these entrance pillars rested in bronze bases at the doorway where worshippers approached.
